Article.ArticleTitle: Deuterium metabolic imaging reveals greater liver fat contribution from lipogenesis in South Asian men than European men: a potential mechanism underlying elevated type 2 diabetes risk.

Abstract.AbstractText: South Asian individuals are up to six times more likely to develop type 2 diabetes than individuals from other ethnic groups, often at a younger age and lower BMI. It has been shown that liver fat accumulates more readily in South Asian individuals, and this is thought to be a key driving factor contributing to the insulin resistance and diabetes in this population. However, the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain unclear. Understanding the role of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) in liver fat accumulation has been hampered by a lack of non-invasive techniques to quantify DNL-derived liver fat. We developed a method to quantify DNL-derived liver fat and used it in a proof-of-concept case-control study, hypothesising that there would be greater liver fat contribution from DNL in South Asian individuals than in European individuals.

A total of seven South Asian and six European participants, matched for age and BMI, underwent deuterium magnetic resonance scans at baseline and after 5 days of 2H water enrichment, from which the fractional and absolute amounts of liver fat from DNL (DNLMR) were calculated. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) and MRI were used to determine lipid quantity and composition.

Our method allowed precise quantification of 2H-labelled liver lipids (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC]>0.956), which enabled us to accurately detect changes in liver fat due to DNL. Both fractional and absolute DNLMR were higher in South Asian participants than in European participants (both p=0.041). DNLMR correlated with liver fat content (fractional rs=0.874, absolute rs=0.888; both p=0.001), as well as the saturation ratio of both liver fat (fractional rs=0.692, absolute rs=0.748; both p<0.05) and visceral adipose tissue (fractional rs=0.648, absolute rs=0.708; both p<0.01). Liver fat content correlated with insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) (rs=0.659, p=0.014).

DNL or related factors may play a pivotal role in driving the increased liver fat and risk of diabetes in South Asian individuals. The novel methodology used to quantify DNL provides a powerful tool for studying DNL-derived liver fat in human metabolic disorders including diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Mitochondrial YME1L Restrains GRP75-Dependent ISR Activation to Prevent Podocyte Senescence in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: Loss of YME1L promotes podocyte senescence in diabetic kidney disease. YME1L deficiency induces sustained maladaptive integrated stress response activation. YME1L interacts with and regulates mitochondrial GRP75 homeostasis. GRP75 accumulation drives persistent integrated stress response activation and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Article.ArticleTitle: CGM-derived disposition index estimates beta cell function in individuals with islet autoimmunity who do not require insulin treatment; changes in the disposition index precede changes identified by CGM metrics 1 year later.

Abstract.AbstractText: Monitoring of beta cell function in individuals with islet autoimmunity who do not require insulin treatment (preclinical type 1 diabetes) is normally done via OGTTs, posing major challenges given the invasiveness of the test. Here, we validated a disposition index (DI) derived from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics (DICGM), which is a proxy of beta cell function, against the gold-standard OGTT DI (DIMM), in a cohort of individuals with one or more islet autoantibodies who do not require insulin treatment.

Participants underwent a 3 h 10-point OGTT with measurement of glucose, insulin and C-peptide while wearing a blinded CGM. The sensor was started 24 h prior to the OGTT. DICGM was computed using CGM data during the 3 h OGTT and two blood glucose calibrations, and compared with the DI from the oral minimal model (DIMM), which uses plasma glucose, insulin and C-peptide. The association between the baseline DICGM and duration of glucose levels above 7.8 mmol/l (140 mg/dl) (TA140) at 1 year was explored.

Twenty-four participants (median age 16.8 years [IQR 13.5-27.7] ) were enrolled, of whom 18 completed both the OGTT (ten with pre-stage 1, seven with stage 1 and one with stage 3a type 1 diabetes) and CGM at baseline, and had repeat CGM 1 year later. The baseline DICGM was highly correlated with the DIMM (r=0.90, p<0.001). Lower baseline DICGM was associated with higher 1 year TA140 (r=-0.61, p=0.014) and higher 1 year mean sensor glucose (r=-0.62, p=0.020).

Beta cell function can be estimated using CGM during a glucose load. DICGM correlates with a 1 year clinically relevant outcome (TA140) in individuals with islet autoimmunity who do not require insulin therapy.

Article.ArticleTitle: Hashimoto's thyroiditis: two decades on.

Abstract.AbstractText: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions and is characterised by immune-mediated injury to thyroid follicular cells. Its pathophysiology involves an interplay of genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, and epigenetic modifications that disrupt immune tolerance, promoting T-cell mediated thyroid injury and thyroid autoantibody production. The disease can progress from euthyroid autoimmunity to subclinical and overt hypothyroidism, with substantial variation in its course. Clinical manifestations vary with the extent of thyroid dysfunction and inflammatory activity. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment, thyroid function testing, thyroid autoantibody measurement, and ultrasonography when indicated. Management centres on levothyroxine replacement for overt hypothyroidism, with an individualised approach to subclinical disease. Thyroidectomy is reserved for selected indications, whereas emerging immunomodulatory strategies remain investigational. This Review synthesises developments over the past two decades in the epidemiology, natural history, aetiopathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and considers emerging mechanistic insights and approaches to precision medicine that might inform future disease-modifying therapies.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Multicenter 13-Week Evaluation of the twiist Automated Insulin Delivery in Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes: The twiist-T2D Pivotal Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and user satisfaction of the twiist automated insulin delivery (AID) system in adults with type 2 diabetes.

In a single-arm, multicenter trial, 307 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 19-85 years old, initiated use of the twiist AID system for 13 weeks after collection of baseline continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data. The primary outcome was change in HbA1c from baseline to 13 weeks.

Mean HbA1c decreased by 0.7% (95% CI -0.9 to -0.6) from 8.1% ± 1.5% at baseline to 7.4% ± 0.9% after using twiist for 13 weeks (P < 0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority). The treatment effect was greatest in participants with baseline HbA1c ≥9.0%. A substantial HbA1c reduction was observed when AID was added to prestudy use of a glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist or sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor drug, which was continued during the trial. Mean CGM-measured time-in-range 70-180 mg/dL increased from 57% ± 26% to 73% ± 17% (mean change 16% [95% CI 14-18]; P < 0.001). All other multiplicity-controlled CGM outcomes reflective of hyperglycemia showed significant improvement from baseline. The frequency of CGM-measured hypoglycemia was low at baseline and remained low during follow-up. Diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in one participant; no severe hypoglycemia events occurred. Using twiist, participant satisfaction was higher than with their prestudy insulin delivery method (P < 0.001) and sleep quality improved (P < 0.001).
In this single-arm, 13-week trial in adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, AID with the twiist system was safe and associated with substantially improved glycemia.

Article.ArticleTitle: Diabetes Care of Children With Type 1 Diabetes at School: Factors Related to the Choice of Care Location and Association With Glycemic Control.

Abstract.AbstractText: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) management in children requires a comprehensive approach tailored to developmental stages and school environments. This study investigated the locations of self-management behaviors at school, examining factors influencing location choice and their associations with glycemic control.

This multicenter, cross-sectional study analyzed 2018 registration data from 1,105 children with T1D attending schools or preschools in Japan. Associations among HbA1c, care behaviors, locations, treatment modalities, age, and sex were statistically evaluated.

The mean (SD) HbA1c was 8.01% (1.12%) (64.0 [12.2] mmol/mol). Care locations were the classroom (36.9%), designated rooms (52.6%), and the restroom (5.9%). HbA1c was significantly higher in the restroom group at 8.56% (0.98%) (70.1 [10.7] mmol/mol) than in the classroom group at 8.00% (1.20%) (63.9 [13.1] mmol/mol) and designated room group at 7.95% (1.08%) (63.4 [11.8] mmol/mol) (P < 0.001). Restroom use and omitting prelunch blood glucose monitoring were independently associated with higher HbA1c. Pump use, continuous glucose monitoring, and male sex predicted higher classroom use and lower restroom use. Joinpoint analysis showed that classroom use declined after age 6 (elementary school entry), whereas restroom use emerged from age 11 and spiked markedly at age 16 (20.8%), coinciding with high school entry, even among pump users.

Care location choice shifts dynamically with age and school transitions, with restroom use being linked to poorer glycemic control. Supporting youth during school transitions requires targeted environmental adjustments and enhanced school-wide understanding to ensure safe and appropriate care locations.

Article.ArticleTitle: Hyperglycemia Drives an Activated, Lipid-Laden Nonclassical Monocyte Phenotype in Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Although monocytes can accumulate lipids, whether diabetes alters monocyte lipid loading is unknown. Nonclassical monocytes accumulate more lipids via a process that is partly regulated by hyperglycemia in people with diabetes and in three different mouse models of diabetes. Increased lipid loading promotes a more activated monocyte phenotype. Nonclassical monocytes contribute to the accumulation of foamy kidney macrophages in a mouse model of diabetic kidney disease.

Article.ArticleTitle: Olive Oil Before Oral Glucose Delays Gastric Emptying and Lowers Glycemia Through Partially Redundant Glucagon and GLP-1 Signaling in Mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: We undertook this study to define how fat consumed before oral glucose attenuates postchallenge glycemia. We asked whether olive oil reduces glycemia by slowing gastric emptying and investigated contributing endocrine and neural pathways. Olive oil increased glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, and glucagon-like peptide-1; slowed gastric emptying; and reduced early glycemia in mice. Glucagon and glucagon-like peptide-1 signaling acted redundantly, with vagal involvement. Nutrient timing integrates endocrine-neural regulation of gastric emptying and glycemia, supporting evaluation of meal sequencing in humans.

Article.ArticleTitle: Continuous Glucose Monitoring-Guided Insulin Optimization in Patients Receiving Nocturnal Parenteral Nutrition.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate whether a continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) system (CGMS)-guided insulin optimization can improve glucose control and nutritional status in insulin-treated patients receiving long-term nocturnal parenteral nutrition (PN).

In this prospective single-center study, 12 insulin-treated adults with chronic intestinal failure undergoing nocturnal cyclic PN underwent 30-day CGM assessment before and after a diabetologist-led optimization of insulin therapy.

Glucose profiles improved after the intervention: less time >250 mg/dL (27% to 17%; -139 ± 113 min/day; P = 0.02), more time in range (44% to 59%; +206 ± 118 min/day; P = 0.002), and without more hypoglycemia. HbA1c decreased by -0.7% (-8 mmol/mol; P = 0.04), and glycosuria resolved in all affected patients (P = 0.03). Body weight increased by +5 kg (interquartile range 4-7.75; P = 0.006), as did serum albumin (+8 g/L; P = 0.006). Malnutrition resolved among 8 of 11 participants (P < 0.05).
CGMS-guided insulin optimization was associated with improvements in glucose control and nutritional status.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Classification Algorithm for Diabetes Subtypes in a Swedish Cohort: Comparison With National Diabetes Register Diagnoses and Genetic Validation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Diabetes subtype-specific research is challenging when using data from large registers, and validation studies of Swedish National Diabetes Register (NDR) diagnoses remain limited. We aimed to develop an algorithm to classify diabetes subtypes using linked longitudinal data, compare with NDR, and validate it using polygenic risk scores. We developed an algorithm that reliably distinguishes diabetes subtypes with higher granularity compared with NDR and is validated by polygenic risk scores. Our algorithm reveals clinically meaningful heterogeneity that may be overlooked in registers and enables subtype-specific diabetes research.

Article.ArticleTitle: Genetic background modulates MafAS64F-mediated islet ageing in male mice.

Abstract.AbstractText: In monogenic diabetes, there is increasing recognition that common polygenic factors can modulate diabetes penetrance beyond the causative mutation(s). A naturally occurring mutation in the gene encoding the essential islet-enriched transcription factor MafA (MafAS64F) produces an unusually long-lived variant protein that predisposes male carriers to MODY. Here we investigated how genetic background modulates disease penetrance in MafaS64F/+ male mice.

MafaS64F/+ male mice, either on a mixed genetic background (C57BL/6J and SJL/J) or backcrossed to a C57BL/6J background, were assessed for glucose levels, beta cell function and gene signatures associated with cellular ageing. RNA-seq analysis was performed to identify unique differentially expressed genes (DEGS) and pathways in mixed-background or C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets. These were overlaid on MafA CUT&RUN peaks to identify direct targets that could differentially impact beta cell function in each background.

MafaS64F/+ male mice on a mixed background manifested overt diabetes, impaired insulin secretion, accelerated beta cell senescence and dysregulated circadian gene expression, while backcross to C57BL/6J prevented dysglycaemia and maintained insulin secretion in MafaS64F/+ male mice, comparable with control littermates. RNA-seq of C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets revealed relative normalisation of DEGs associated with cellular ageing and circadian regulation. In addition, islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice showed unique downregulation of retinoic acid signalling and cell cycle inhibitor p21, the latter of which modulates cellular ageing and diabetes seen in the mixed-background mouse islets. CUT&RUN mapping revealed that MafA directly impacted expression of (at least) retinoic acid receptor-α (encoded by Rara) in islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice and circadian regulation in islets from mixed-background mice.

In sum, these data show that genetic modifiers can impact beta cell regulation of retinoic acid signalling and circadian entrainment to modulate beta cell ageing and disease penetrance in mice modelling MAFA-MODY.

Sequencing data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (accession no. GSE299343 for bulk RNA-seq and GSE298664 for CUT&RUN analyses).

Article.ArticleTitle: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Across Renal Compartments in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: Mitochondrial dysfunction in diabetic kidney disease is compartment and stage specific, reflecting differences in renal cell metabolism, function, and injury response. This article introduces a framework for interpreting mitochondrial dysfunction across renal cell types and disease stages. Proximal tubular stress progresses from increased transport demand to mitochondrial injury and impaired quality control. Distal nephron, immune, and interstitial mitochondrial mechanisms remain incompletely defined. In glomerular endothelial cells and podocytes, mitochondria primarily regulate stress and injury signaling. Cell-specific mitochondrial phenotyping may reveal reversible pathways and guide more precise therapeutic strategies in diabetic kidney disease.

Article.ArticleTitle: Glucose controls metallothionein 1 gene expression in pancreatic islets via a mechanism involving cellular metabolism, granular zinc and the zinc transporter ZnT8 in rat and mouse.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metallothionein 1 (MT1) negatively regulates insulin secretion in pancreatic beta cells, and is upregulated by low non-stimulating glucose levels compared with physiological glucose stimulation in cultured rodent and human islets. Whether this regulation also occurs in vivo and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here we examine whether physiological changes in blood glucose levels in vivo control islet Mt1 gene expression similarly to ex vivo observations, and identify the mechanisms involved.

Rats fasted for 1, 2 or 3 days and rats fasted for 2 days and refed for 1 day were compared with rats fed throughout. Mice implanted with subcutaneous insulin mini-osmotic pumps were compared with control mice. Rat and mouse islets were cultured in the presence of optimal glucose levels (10 mmol/l; G10 medium) or low non-stimulating glucose levels (2 or 5 mmol/l; G2 or G5 medium) in the absence or presence of various modulators of mitochondrial metabolism, protein synthesis, Ca2+ influx, autophagy and insulin secretion. Islets from Znt8 (Slc30a8) knockout (KO) mice and corresponding control mice were studied. Gene mRNA levels were assessed by reverse-transcription followed by real-time PCR, plasma and secreted insulin levels were assessed using RIA, intracellular free Zn2+ ([Zn2+]c) was assessed using FluoZin-3, metal regulatory transcription factor 1 (MTF1) activity was assessed using an MTF1-luciferase lentiviral reporter system, and beta cell morphology was assessed by transmission electron microscopy.

Among glucose-affected zinc transporters/importers in rat islets, only the zinc efflux transporter Znt1 (Slc30a1) was upregulated under low non-stimulating glucose levels (G2 and G5 medium) vs physiological glucose stimulation (G10 medium), in parallel with Mt1. In vivo, Mt1 mRNA levels were upregulated approximately 3-4-fold in the islets of fasted rats and mice implanted with insulin pumps, with both conditions inducing sustained hypoglycaemia. This effect was fully reversed after normalisation of blood glucose levels. Interestingly, Znt1 mRNA levels changed in parallel with those of Mt1. Hypoglycaemia also markedly altered the expression of beta cell-enriched genes (downregulated), adaptive unfolded protein response (UPR) genes (downregulated), integrated stress response (ISR)/proapoptotic UPR genes (upregulated) and oxidative stress-responsive genes (upregulated). Normalisation of blood glucose levels largely reversed these alterations. In cultured islets, addition to G2 medium of mitochondrial metabolic substrates that bypass glycolysis inhibited Mt1 expression to the same extent as G10 medium. Conversely, the reduction of Mt1 expression in G10 medium was prevented when mitochondrial function or protein synthesis were inhibited. In comparison with fed mice, beta cells of fasted mice had degradative autophagic vacuoles containing secretory granule components. In agreement, islet cells cultured in G2 vs G10 medium showed an increase in [Zn2+]c that was prevented by chloroquine treatment. Co-staining with nuclear and cytosolic markers confirmed the cytosolic and perinuclear subcellular localisation of increased [Zn2+]c in G2 medium. This effect was reproduced in MIN6 cells cultured in G5 vs G25 medium (containing 25 mmol/l glucose, which is the optimal concentration for culture of MIN6 cells) and was paralleled by a significant increase in MTF1 activity, which is a robust indicator of an increase in cytosolic free Zn2+. In Znt8-KO islets, the depletion of zinc from secretory granules prevented the increase in [Zn2+]c and the upregulation of islet Mt1 and other MTF1-regulated genes (Mt2 and Znt1) by low glucose levels.

Physiological changes in glucose levels dynamically regulate islet Mt1 gene expression in vivo as previously shown ex vivo. Mt1 downregulation by glucose depends on active mitochondrial metabolism and protein synthesis, and correlates with reduced [Zn2+]c and MTF1 activity. Its upregulation under low glucose is associated with autophagic degradation of insulin granules, release of intragranular Zn2+ into the cytosol, an increase in [Zn2+]c, and increased MTF1 activity. This upregulation is absent in Znt8-KO islets, thereby demonstrating that it requires a functional ZnT8 transporter. Our findings establish a novel link between MT1 and ZnT8, and shift our understanding of Mt1 regulation from a simple stress-dependent mechanism to a more complex model involving the modulation of cellular metabolism and intracellular zinc dynamics.

Article.ArticleTitle: Contemporary Sex-Specific Mortality Risk in Type 1 Diabetes During the Era of Advanced Therapeutic Care.

Abstract.AbstractText: Amid major advances in diabetes care technologies, this study aimed to assess all-cause mortality risk among individuals diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in recent decades compared with matched control individuals.

This retrospective cohort study included all patients with type 1 diabetes diagnosed before age 35 between 2000 and 2022, identified through a validated registry from Maccabi Healthcare Services (MHS), a large state-mandated health care provider network. A diabetes-free comparison cohort was constructed using 1:4 propensity score matching by sex and age. Follow-up continued until 2023, death, or transfer from MHS, whichever occurred first. Cox regression and sensitivity analyses were performed.

Mortality rates among 4,299 individuals with type 1 diabetes (mean ± SD age at diagnosis, 17.4 ± 9.1 years) and 17,196 matched control individuals (45.6% female overall) were 131.0 and 35.2 per 100,000 person-years, respectively, with 112 deaths over 204,102 person-years. Type 1 diabetes was associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio [HR] 3.66; 95% CI 2.53-5.31), with consistent estimates after adjustment and sensitivity analyses. Excess mortality was greater in females than males (adjusted HR 8.40 [3.71-19.04] vs. 2.90 [1.78-4.72]; P-interaction = 0.02), although absolute mortality rates were higher in males. Mortality risk was higher in those diagnosed in 2000-2010 than in 2011-2022 (adjusted HR 4.36 [1.22-15.57] vs. 2.94 [1.31-6.60]), with follow-up truncated for comparability.
Type 1 diabetes was associated with higher risk of mortality, particularly among females. This association was attenuated among individuals diagnosed in more recent years.

Article.ArticleTitle: Skeletal Muscle DPT Ameliorates Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction via the PERK/eIF2α/ATF4-GDF15 Axis.

Abstract.AbstractText: We identified dermatopontin (DPT) as a previously unrecognized compensatory regulator that is upregulated in skeletal muscle in obesity and preserves muscle function and systemic metabolic homeostasis, offering a potential therapeutic target for metabolic disorders. Mechanistically, DPT activates an adaptive PERK/eIF2α/ATF4 endoplasmic reticulum stress axis specifically under metabolic stress, but not under normal conditions, which enhances muscle function and directly counteracts metabolic deterioration, revealing a protective signaling cascade. This DPT-driven endoplasmic reticulum stress axis transcriptionally upregulates growth differentiation factor (GDF) 15 expression and secretion in muscle. Muscle-derived GDF15 exerts both local muscle-autonomous and systemic protective effects, uncovering a previously unrecognized muscle-to-organ cross-talk axis.

Article.ArticleTitle: Efficacy and safety of HRS-7535, a novel oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, in participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled by metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase II trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HRS-7535, an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), in Chinese participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately managed by metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i).

This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase II study included participants aged 18-75 years with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 58-97 mmol/mol (7.5-11.0%) and BMI 20.0-35.0 kg/m2 and on stable-dose metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor therapy for ≥8 weeks prior to screening. Participants were assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive HRS-7535 30 mg, HRS-7535 60 mg or visually matching placebo tablets once daily using a stratified block randomisation method, with treatment assignments concealed until study completion. The primary endpoint was the change in HbA1c from baseline to week 16. Secondary efficacy outcomes included the proportions of participants achieving HbA1c targets of <53 mmol/mol (7.0%) and ≤48 mmol/mol (6.5%), and changes from baseline in fasting body weight to week 16.

A total of 155 participants with a mean baseline HbA1c of 69 mmol/mol (8.5%) were randomly assigned to HRS-7535 30 mg (n=51), HRS-7535 60 mg (n=53) or placebo (n=51). At week 16, the least‑squares mean differences in HbA1c from baseline for the HRS-7535 30 mg, HRS-7535 60 mg and placebo groups were -16 mmol/mol (95% CI -19, -14) (-1.5% [95% CI -1.7, -1.3]), -20 mmol/mol (95% CI -22, -17) (-1.8% [95% CI -2.0, -1.6]) and -4 mmol/mol (95% CI -7, -2) (-0.4% [95% CI -0.6, -0.2]), respectively (p<0.0001 for both HRS-7535 doses vs placebo). The proportions of participants achieving HbA1c <53 mmol/mol (7.0%) were 51.0% in the HRS‑7535 30 mg group, 66.0% in the HRS‑7535 60 mg group, and 9.8% in the placebo group; the corresponding proportions for HbA1c ≤48 mmol/mol (6.5%) were 35.3%, 37.7% and 3.9%, respectively. Body weight loss was -2.4% in the HRS-7535 60 mg group vs -0.7% in the placebo group. Most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild to moderate, and gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common. No severe hypoglycaemia was reported. The only TEAE that led to treatment discontinuation occurred in the placebo group.

Treatment with HRS-7535 resulted in significant improvements in glycaemic management in participants with type 2 diabetes, and the drug exhibited a favourable safety profile. To address a significant clinical data void, this research focused on the addition of HRS‑7535 to the background regimen of metformin and SGLT2i for glycaemic management in participants with type 2 diabetes. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06393348. Funding This study was funded by Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals.

Article.ArticleTitle: Reversal of T1D and Rapid Reduction of β-Cell Stress by IL-10-Dependent MDSCs Induced by TLR4-Ab.

Abstract.AbstractText: Therapy with IgG3 Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD2) agonistic antibody (TLR4-Ab) is a novel approach to type 1 diabetes (T1D) immunotherapy that targets the innate immune system by inducing immunoregulatory myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). We sought to define the mechanisms by which TLR4-Ab induces MDSCs and how they reverse T1D. TLR4-Ab induction of MDSCs requires interleukin 10 signaling in the bone marrow, and MDSCs mediate suppression via inducible nitric oxide synthase. Induction of immunoregulatory MDSCs results in profound downregulation of β-cell endoplasmic reticulum stress and unfolded protein response associated with acute T1D. Establishing mechanisms by which TLR4-Ab reverses acute T1D defines new therapeutic pathways for human T1D that target innate immunity to restore immune tolerance.

Article.ArticleTitle: Correction to Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2026; 14: 894-902.
An Incretin-Dependent Modulation of Periprandial Neutrophilia.

Abstract.AbstractText: We determine how innate immunity adapts to transitions between fasting and feeding. Feeding rapidly induced periprandial neutrophilia. HFD accelerated this reponse. We therefore sought to examine whether periprandial states regulate neutrophil dynamics. We identified that the glucagon-like peptide 1 and insulin axis modulates the neutrophil surge, which is critical during endotoxin challenges. The periprandial state prepares the host for endotoxemia. We bridge nutrient intake and incretin-sensitive immunity to inflammatory tone, redefining postprandial inflammation, insulin resistance, and cardiometabolic risk in diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Altered glucagon and GIP responses in South Asian versus Nordic women after gestational diabetes mellitus.

Abstract.AbstractText: We aimed to compare ethnic differences in levels of glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) following a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and to assess whether the higher insulin levels observed in South Asian compared with Nordic women could be explained by differences in the hormone secretory responses.

We measured glucagon, GIP and GLP-1 in 178 South Asian and 107 Nordic women during an OGTT, and stratified participants by glycaemic status. Glucagon and total GLP-1 and GIP responses when fasting and post-OGTT were assessed by linear mixed models. Ethnic differences in incretin and glucagon levels were evaluated by linear regression analyses. Pre-hepatic insulin levels were estimated using deconvolution of C-peptide kinetics.

Ethnic differences in glucagon and incretin levels varied by glycaemic status. In the normoglycaemic South Asian group, early (0-15 min) glucagon suppression post-OGTT was significantly attenuated compared with the Nordic group (p=0.002). Fasting glucagon levels did not differ (p=0.139), but total glucagon exposure (including fasting levels) was higher in South Asian women (p=0.013). No differences in GIP and GLP responses to the OGTT were observed (p=0.490 and p=0.802). In women with prediabetes or diabetes, fasting glucagon was higher in the South Asian group (p=0.010), but there were no significant differences in early glucagon suppression post-OGTT (p=0.986). GIP responses to the OGTT were lower among South Asian women (p<0.001), despite higher insulin responses compared with the Nordic women. GLP-1 responses did not differ between the ethnic groups (p=0.661). The higher pre-hepatic insulin levels in South Asian vs Nordic normoglycaemic women were not associated with differences in incretin levels, but were associated with lower insulin sensitivity in the regression analyses (p<0.001).

When examined 1-3 years post-GDM, normoglycaemic South Asian women had less early glucagon suppression and higher total glucagon exposure post-OGTT compared with Nordic women. The higher pre-hepatic insulin levels were not associated with higher incretin levels, but were associated with lower insulin sensitivity.

Article.ArticleTitle: Evolving phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a 15-year population-based comparison.

Abstract.AbstractText: Our aim was to describe the phenotype at diagnosis and the early therapeutic profile of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes across two periods spanning approximately 15 years within the same integrated healthcare system.

This retrospective cohort study used electronic health record data from Clalit Health Services (Haifa & Western Galilee, Israel). Adults with incident type 2 diabetes in 2005-2008 (period 1: n=80,201) were compared with those diagnosed in 2020-2023 (period 2: n=101,392). Between-period differences are presented as crude estimates, with an age-stratified sensitivity analysis, and quantified using standardised mean differences (SMDs; values ≥0.20 indicate at least a small effect) alongside non-parametric and χ2 tests.

The median age at diagnosis increased from 63.0 to 66.7 years between the two periods; the proportion aged ≥85 years nearly doubled (from 3.5% to 6.6%). The score for the Charlson comorbidity index increased from 4 to 6 (SMD 0.48); metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) increased from 4.4% to 18.6%. HbA1c at diagnosis decreased from 56 to 53 mmol/mol (7.3% to 7.0%); pre-diagnosis LDL-cholesterol decreased from 2.90 to 2.21 mmol/l (SMD 0.65). Within 31-90 days of diagnosis, use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors increased from 0.07% to 15.0%, use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) increased from 0% to 11.1%, and sulfonylurea use decreased more than fourfold (20.8% to 4.5%).

The phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes has been fundamentally restructured since 2008: patients are older with a higher comorbidity burden but present with better glycaemic and lipid management, with the latter reflecting statin therapy already established before diagnosis. MASLD has emerged as a major but largely ascertainment-driven comorbidity. The shift to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs alongside declining sulfonylurea use indicates displacement of glucose-centric strategies by a cardiorenal- and weight-driven paradigm. These findings indicate a need for age-appropriate management and trials enrolling very elderly patients.

Article.ArticleTitle: Prediabetes subtype-based stratification reveals distinct long-term risks for type 2 diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Prediabetes is heterogeneous, with subtypes defined by impaired fasting glucose (IFG), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or HbA1c, each with different risks of progression to type 2 diabetes. We compared progression across these subtypes, and evaluated the benefit of adding insulin secretion and sensitivity to risk stratification.

We analysed 7186 Korean adults aged 40-69 years from the community-based Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study, who were followed for up to 20 years with biennial (every 2 years) oral glucose tolerance tests and HbA1c. Prediabetes was classified as IFG, IGT or HbA1c-defined, and further stratified by insulinogenic index (IGI) and insulin sensitivity index (ISI). Cox regression was used to estimate diabetes risk, and multistate Markov models were used to assess annual transition probabilities and time spent in each state.

Compared with normoglycaemia, the adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were 5.84 (95% CI 5.03, 6.79) for IFG, 4.60 (95% CI 4.17, 5.07) for IGT, and 4.68 (95% CI 4.22, 5.19) for HbA1c-defined prediabetes. The risk increased stepwise with the number of criteria met: the aHRs were 3.10 (95% CI 2.81, 3.41) for one criterion, 7.33 (95% CI 6.50, 8.28) for two criteria, and 15.3 (95% CI 12.2, 19.3) for all three. Markov models showed the shortest prediabetes duration (1.7 years) and lowest regression probability (5.4%) in those meeting all three criteria. Low IGI or ISI predicted higher diabetes risk, and dual impairment conferred greatest risk (aHR 4.06; 95% CI 3.37, 4.90). Even normoglycaemic individuals with low IGI or ISI had an elevated risk of diabetes compared to those with high IGI or ISI.

Diabetes progression differs based on both glycaemic subtype and physiological subtype. Integrating IGI and ISI with conventional definitions enhances risk stratification and may help to identify high-risk individuals for earlier targeted intervention.

Article.ArticleTitle: Renal tubule-specific Nrf2 deletion ameliorates diabetic kidney disease by attenuating glomerular hypertension and kidney injury in a mouse model of diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: We previously reported that expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) is upregulated in the renal tubules of humans with diabetes and in mouse models of diabetes. We hypothesised that Nrf2 deletion would ameliorate renal hyperfiltration and kidney injury in Akita mice (a model of type 1 diabetes).

Akita Nrf2RT knockout (KO) mice were generated by cross-breeding tubule-specific (Pax8)-Cre mice with Akita Nrf2 floxed mice on a C57BL/6 background. Male non-diabetic control mice (Nrf2fl/fl), Nrf2RT KO mice, Akita Nrf2fl/fl mice and Akita Nrf2RT KO mice were studied up to the age of 20 weeks (n=8 per group).

The glomerular filtration rate (GFR), kidney hypertrophy, tubular injury score, glomerular basement membrane thickness, podocyte loss and foot process effacement and urinary albumin-creatinine ratio were significantly increased in Akita Nrf2fl/fl mice and were markedly reduced in Akita Nrf2RT KO mice compared with the corresponding control mice. Attenuation of afferent arteriole vasodilation and efferent arteriole vasoconstriction was observed in Akita Nrf2RT KO mice compared with Akita Nrf2fl/fl mice. Furthermore, downregulation of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) and angiotensinogen expression in renal proximal tubules was observed in Akita Nrf2RT KO mice compared with Akita Nrf2fl/fl mice. Treatment of Akita Nrf2RT KO mice with a selective A1 adenosine receptor inhibitor increased GFR and fractional excretion of glucose, suggesting that enhanced adenosine signalling may contribute to the altered renal haemodynamics through tubuloglomerular feedback and reduced glomerular injury associated with RT-specific Nrf2 deletion.

These findings suggest that tubular NRF2 plays an important role in the progression of diabetic kidney disease in Akita mice through modulation of the GFR and expression of SGLT2 and angiotensinogen in renal proximal tubules and tubuloglomerular feedback.

Article.ArticleTitle: Amino Acid Profiles Distinguish Glycemic Phenotypes in Childhood and Predict 10-Year Risk of Dysglycemia in Young Adults: The BCAMS Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Prospective evidence linking childhood amino acid (AA) dysregulation with future diabetes risk remains limited. We examined whether AA profiles distinguished childhood glycemic phenotypes and predicted dysglycemia risk in the Beijing Children and Adolescents Metabolic Syndrome (BCAMS) cohort. AA alterations were already detectable in children with normoglycemia and insulin resistance; six AAs were associated with 10-year dysglycemia risk, and their addition to clinical variables improved prediction. Ile showed the largest estimated indirect association with incident dysglycemia through follow-up insulin resistance; dietary Ile restriction in obese mice produced concordant metabolic changes, supporting AA profiling for early risk identification and Ile as a candidate modifiable target.

Article.ArticleTitle: The development of obesity pharmacotherapy: from early challenges and setbacks to recognition by WHO.

Abstract.AbstractText: Obesity is a chronic, progressive disease associated with disability, increased morbidity, and reduced life expectancy. Global prevalence has risen sharply in recent decades, yet obesity and its treatment-particularly pharmacotherapy -have been highly stigmatised. A legacy of early medications withdrawn over safety concerns, together with poor efficacy, and widespread lack of recognition of obesity as a chronic disease contributed to persistent underuse of obesity pharmacotherapy. This underuse changed in the 2020s with GLP-1 receptor agonists and, later, multiagonist therapies, with their substantially greater efficacy, safety, and disease-modifying benefits compared with older agents. Reflecting this paradigm shift, WHO issued global guidelines and included GLP-1 receptor agonists in the Essential Medicines List, albeit for a narrowly defined population. We take a critical historical perspective, charting the highs and lows of obesity medication development and examining the scientific, regulatory, and societal factors that have slowed or impeded the translation of pharmacological advances into safe, effective, and widely accepted treatments for obesity.

Article.ArticleTitle: CCKBR signalling controls human definitive endoderm specification and pancreatic lineage differentiation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Paracrine signalling by hormone-producing endocrine cells potentially influences pancreatic development, but this feedback regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the roles of gastrin (GAST), cholecystokinin (CCK) and their receptor cholecystokinin B receptor (CCKBR) during human pancreatic development.

Human iPSCs were differentiated stepwise into definitive endoderm and then the pancreatic endocrine lineage. To assess CCKBR function, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate CCKBR-knockout iPSC lines. We profiled transcriptional states by bulk and single-cell RNA-seq with computational analyses, and complemented these with biochemical assays, flow cytometry (FACS) and confocal microscopy.

CCKBR expression peaked during definitive endoderm formation and progressively declined during differentiation, remaining detectable in pancreatic progenitors but largely absent from the endocrine lineage. By contrast, GAST and CCK were expressed only transiently during pancreatic progenitor and endocrine lineage formation. Pharmacological activation/inhibition and genetic knockout implicated CCKBR signalling during definitive endoderm formation. Consistently, bulk RNA-seq indicated that CCKBR deletion triggered ectodermal- and mesodermal-associated transcriptional programs and diminished pancreatic lineage specification. During pancreatic induction and lineage formation, sustained CCKBR activation with GAST or CCK attenuated endocrinogenesis and promoted epithelial structure formation. Further analysis revealed the emergence of a pancreatic ductal-like cell formation under prolonged CCKBR stimulation.

This study provides mechanistic evidence that the GAST/CCK-CCKBR axis is functionally important during human endoderm and pancreas development. This pathway is repeatedly required during in vitro pluripotent stem cell differentiation, regulating germ-layer formation as well as ductal vs endocrine fate decisions. These findings support the optimisation of pancreatic differentiation protocols and inform future studies on whether this axis contributes to human pancreas development and disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: We investigated whether an association existed between epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) in type 1 diabetes, using 10 clocks and two cohorts, and whether this amplified disease progression. Older EAA phenotypic age and shorter epigenetically predicted telomere lengths were significantly associated with DKD. Progression from normolbuminuria to severely increased albuminuria was associated with increased EAA, and age, epigenetic age, and EAA were significant predictors of progression to end-stage kidney disease. Results support the development of epigenetic biomarkers predicting DKD onset and progression.

Article.ArticleTitle: Clinical Trial Design Considerations for the Development of Disease-Modifying Therapies for Type 1 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Several disease-modifying therapies have reduced the progressive loss of β-cell function in type 1 diabetes, with efficacy observed across a wide array of underlying therapeutic mechanisms of action. These successes highlight opportunities to accelerate the development of novel and repurposed type 1 diabetes treatments; however, only one such therapy has received regulatory approval for clinical use and few phase 3 clinical trials have been performed. For bringing emerging therapies to people living with type 1 diabetes as quickly and efficiently as possible, overall regulatory strategy and clinical trial design, especially inclusion criteria and end point selection, are essential, and planning must include their careful consideration. The considerations discussed herein represent a feasible and promising road map for developers of disease-modifying therapies and establish that type 1 diabetes remains a promising area for continued investment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolic-bariatric surgery (MBS) is effective in promoting remission of type 2 diabetes, but this outcome is not universally achieved. We identified baseline patient characteristics that predict diabetes remission and subsequent relapse after various MBS procedures versus intensive medical-lifestyle intervention.

Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D) is a 14-year, multicenter study of health outcomes in 262 patients with type 2 diabetes (68% women, age 49.9 ± 8.3 years, BMI 36.4 ± 3.5 kg/m2, HbA1c 8.5 ± 1.5%) previously randomized to MBS (n = 166) or medical-lifestyle management (n = 96). Predictors of remission (defined as HbA1c <6.5% on no glucose-lowering medications) and relapse were determined using univariate time-to-event analyses of prespecified candidate predictors plus agnostic, multivariate least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.

Throughout a median of 11 years (maximum 14 years) of follow-up, 58% of participants randomized to MBS achieved diabetes remission versus 3% with medical-lifestyle management. Predictors of diabetes remission in univariate analyses included shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, fewer glucose-lowering medication classes used, greater body weight, higher fasting C-peptide and insulin levels, and weight loss at 1 year (all P < 0.05). Diabetes remission predictors in multivariate analyses included baseline diabetes duration, insulin use, and weight change at 1 year (all P < 0.01). Diabetes relapse after initial remission in the MBS group was predicted by longer baseline diabetes duration and greater number of glucose-lowering medication classes used.

Baseline predictors of diabetes remission and subsequent relapse among participants randomized to one of three MBS procedures or a medical-lifestyle intervention should help inform personalized selection of diabetes treatment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Low-Carbohydrate Diets, Nutritional Adequacy, Glycemia, and Perinatal Outcomes in Women With Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Secondary Analysis of the DiGest Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: The optimal dietary carbohydrate intake for pregnant women is disputed internationally. Many authorities recommend a minimum of 175 g/day of carbohydrates primarily to support maternal brain glucose requirements and normal fetal brain development. We assessed whether low (<175 g/day) or very low (<120 g/day) carbohydrate intake was associated with altered nutrient intake, glycemia, or pregnancy outcomes in women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).

Women recruited to the Dietary Intervention in Gestational Diabetes Trial (DiGest) completed masked continuous glucose monitoring and a 24-h dietary recall at baseline before random assignment to receive either a standard- (2,000 kcal/day) or reduced-energy diet (1,200 kcal/day) from ∼29-36 weeks' gestation.

At baseline, 215 women completed a dietary assessment, of whom 66 (30.7%), 74 (34.4%), and 75 (34.9%) reported standard (≥175 g/day), low (120-175 g/day), and very low carbohydrate intake (<120 g/day), respectively. Women consuming fewer carbohydrates consumed less energy, less dietary fiber, and fewer vitamins (B and E) and minerals but proportionally more protein and fat. Consumption of <120 g/day carbohydrates as assessed at baseline before the intervention was associated with a lower time above range (TAR) >120 mg/dL (-6.8% [95% CI -13.4% to -0.2%]; P = 0.044) and lower birth weight (-9.6 [95% CI -18.7 to -0.6] centiles; P = 0.037), but no difference in large- or small-for-gestational-age birth weight was observed. Low carbohydrate intake as a proportion of total energy intake (<35%) without energy restriction was associated with reduced TAR but not with a difference in birth weight.

Lower carbohydrate intake at baseline was associated with modestly improved glycemia before random assignment in women with GDM, but vigilance to maintain adequate intake of micronutrients and fiber is required.

Article.ArticleTitle: Revisiting the β-Cell: The Key to the Type 2 Diabetes Puzzle: The 2025 Banting Medal for Scientific Achievement Award Lecture.

Abstract.AbstractText: Major discoveries in the past have laid the foundation on which modern diabetes research has been built, and future findings can be anticipated. From this groundwork, we have pursued studies evaluating the role of β-cell function and β-cell mass in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes. In considering β-cell function, studies of β-cell responses to intravenous and oral glucose have highlighted the critical nature of interpreting these responses in the face of the prevailing insulin sensitivity, and not as isolated responses. The critical role of β-cell dysfunction in the pathogenesis of prediabetes and diabetes has become apparent. When prediabetes is present, β-cell function is reduced by 40%, while in recent-onset type 2 diabetes it is reduced by >80%. In youth with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, β-cell function deteriorates at a faster rate than in adults, compatible with their disease being more aggressive. From clinical trials in both age groups, the progression of β-cell dysfunction over time is the basis for deteriorating glycemia, with none of the currently available glucose-lowering agents able to halt this inexorable decline. Reflecting on β-cell mass, this is clearly reduced in people with type 2 diabetes. One basis for this is islet amyloid, which is formed from the normal β-cell secretory peptide islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) (or amylin). The process of amyloid formation promotes oxidative stress, inflammation, and β-cell death, creating a destructive feed-forward that exacerbates disease progression. Experimental studies demonstrate that reducing amyloid formation reduces oxidative stress, inflammation, and the loss of β-cell mass. Ultimately, preserving β-cell function and mass is critical in striving to prevent and treat type 2 diabetes. Future tactics have to deviate from the current approaches if we are going to be successful in reducing the deleterious effects of a dysfunctional β-cell in type 2 diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Recipe for Better Diabetes Management: The DASH4D Dietary Pattern.

Abstract.AbstractText: The 2026 American Diabetes Association "Standards of Care in Diabetes" includes extensive nutrition recommendations for people with diabetes but stops short of recommending a specific dietary pattern. Instead, the guidelines recommend that all patients be referred for individualized nutrition therapy. This approach appropriately acknowledges diverse patient needs; however, it is difficult for providers to deliver any form of individualized dietary guidance without a clear starting point to guide them. In this article we examine the tension between the needs for individualization and evidence-based nutritional standards in diabetes care. We argue that the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) dietary pattern stands out as being supported by decades of evidence from rigorous randomized clinical trials, meta-analyses, and large observational studies that have established its benefit for cardiovascular health. We summarize the recently completed DASH for Diabetes (DASH4D) trial, which demonstrated that a modified version of the original DASH eating plan, adapted for adults with diabetes, significantly reduced blood pressure and improved glycemic control in participants with type 2 diabetes and hypertension. We conclude that while individualized dietary counseling remains the standard of care, the DASH4D diet should be a recommended diet for patients with diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Novel Protein Biomarkers to Monitor Kidney Function Decline and Treatment Response in Individuals With Normoalbuminuria and Type 2 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Kidney function can decline in individuals with type 2 diabetes despite normal albuminuria, yet current risk stratification relies heavily on urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), which may inadequately capture this process. We investigated whether biomarkers reflecting inflammation, tubular injury, regenerative capacity, and fibrosis improve risk prediction and treatment monitoring beyond UACR in these individuals. Baseline UACR did not predict the composite kidney outcome, whereas TNFR-1, TNFR-2, KIM-1, and MMP-7 were independently associated. In those who developed the outcome, these biomarkers and uEGF/Cr showed divergent trajectories, unlike UACR. Biomarkers capturing pathways beyond glomerular injury may improve risk stratification and treatment monitoring in these normoalbuminuric patients.

Article.ArticleTitle: Protective Effects of PD-L1-Overexpressing MSCs and Their Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Type 1 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study was conducted to address the urgent need for novel therapies for type 1 diabetes. We investigated whether programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-overexpressing mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (PD-L1-MSCs) and their extracellular vesicles (PEVs) can modulate immune responses and protect pancreatic islets, and whether these effects depend on PD-L1 signaling. Our results demonstrate that both PD-L1-MSCs and PEVs suppress T-cell activity, enhance regulatory T-cell populations, delay the onset of diabetes, and reduce immune cell infiltration in pancreatic islets. These findings suggest that PD-L1-MSCs and PEVs represent promising therapeutic strategies for type 1 diabetes by promoting immune tolerance and preserving β-cell function.

Article.ArticleTitle: A prospective controlled study assessing postpartum breastfeeding in women with type 2 diabetes: lower rates associated with elevated BMI rather than diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Breastfeeding is associated with metabolic benefits for women with type 2 diabetes and their infants, yet breastfeeding rates in these women are poorly described. Obesity is associated with type 2 diabetes and lower breastfeeding rates, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of type 2 diabetes vs obesity on breastfeeding. The primary objective was to examine breastfeeding rates in women with type 2 diabetes compared with normoglycaemic women with either (1) matched BMI or (2) normal BMI. The secondary objective was to examine variables associated with breastfeeding.

Pregnant women with type 2 diabetes (cases) or normoglycaemia (controls) were prospectively recruited. Each case was matched with two controls by age and parity and either (1) matched or (2) normal (18-25 kg/m2) BMI. Data were collected from in-person surveys antenatally, medical records and a 4 month postpartum telephone survey. Analysis included descriptive and inferential statistics.

Four months of breastfeeding data were available for 29 women with type 2 diabetes, 29 BMI-matched controls and 28 normal-BMI controls. Breastfeeding rates were similar in women with type 2 diabetes and BMI-matched controls, but both rates were significantly lower than those in normal-BMI controls. 'Full' breastfeeding rates were 24%, 38% and 64% in women with type 2 diabetes, BMI-matched controls and normal-BMI controls, respectively, and were not different between women with type 2 diabetes vs BMI-matched controls (p=0.26) but were lower in women with type 2 diabetes vs normal-BMI controls (p=0.002). 'Any' breastfeeding rates were 55%, 54% and 82% in women with type 2 diabetes, BMI-matched controls and normal-BMI controls, respectively, again showing no difference between women with type 2 diabetes vs BMI-matched controls (p=0.79) but were lower in women with type 2 diabetes vs normal-BMI controls (p=0.03).
Maternal obesity, rather than type 2 diabetes, may be the major determinant of reduced breastfeeding rates 4 months postpartum.

Article.ArticleTitle: Different Patterns of Progression in Nonproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy: Findings From a 10-Year Cohort Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Characterization of the 10-year progression of diabetic retinopathy in type 2 diabetes was sought. We evaluated whether noninvasive optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) can identify eyes that progress and may develop vision loss. Of 222 participants, 62% completed the study, with 115 reaching the 10-year visit: 27% of eyes worsened, 50% remained stable, and 21% improved, based on Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study severity grading (2% unclassified); microvascular nonperfusion, measured using noninvasive OCTA, distinguished the eyes that worsened or remained stable from those eyes that improved. Progression of microvascular nonperfusion identified by OCTA enables identification of patients at higher risk for disease progression.

Article.ArticleTitle: Prediabetes and diabetes as drivers of fibrosis in MASLD: roles of obesity, adipose tissue dysfunction and insulin resistance.

Abstract.AbstractText: Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes have been associated with more severe metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but not all individuals have the same risk and the metabolic drivers remain incompletely understood. To understand why, we examined the roles of obesity, adipose tissue dysfunction and insulin resistance in the development of significant liver fibrosis (fibrosis stage ≥F2) in adults across the glycaemic spectrum.

We performed a prospective, cross-sectional study in a real-world setting of adults attending primary care or endocrinology/diabetes clinics. Transient elastography was used to diagnose steatosis (controlled attenuation parameter ≥274 dB/m) and clinically significant liver fibrosis (vibration-controlled transient elastography liver stiffness measurement ≥8.2 kPa). When ≥F2 was suspected, MR-based imaging or liver biopsy was used to improve stratification. MASLD and significant fibrosis were compared across glycaemic and BMI categories and severity of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR; predominantly hepatic) and adipose tissue insulin resistance (assessed by adipose tissue insulin resistance [Adipo-IR]).

Among the 1446 participants, the prevalence of MASLD increased across glycaemic categories from 39% in participants with normoglycaemia, to 55% in those with prediabetes and to 68% in type 2 diabetes. Clinically significant fibrosis also increased across groups, being 1%, 6% and 12%, respectively. In prediabetes, clinically significant fibrosis was rare in lean or overweight individuals even though most had associated cardiometabolic risk factors, but this increased fourfold in individuals with obesity, particularly when associated with severe adipose tissue and systemic insulin resistance. Having obesity and type 2 diabetes had the highest prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis (16%), and again, mostly if associated with insulin resistance. Most participants with clinically significant fibrosis were in the highest quintiles of Adipo-IR or HOMA-IR (Q4-Q5).

In a real-world cohort from primary care/endocrinology clinics, the prevalence of MASLD increased in a stepwise manner with glycaemic and BMI categories, but the prevalence of fibrosis did not increase in the same stepwise manner and remained rare in the absence of obesity, or in obesity without significant insulin resistance. Prediabetes was a risk factor for significant fibrosis mainly in individuals with obesity and significant insulin resistance. In the context of current guidelines, MASLD risk-stratification may be improved in primary care by establishing the metabolic impact of obesity/diabetes (i.e. assessing insulin resistance by HOMA-IR).

Article.ArticleTitle: Long-term Glycemia and Risk of Death in Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes: A UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Mortality risk is increased in cystic fibrosis (CF)-related diabetes, but its relationship with long-term glycemia is unclear.

Using UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry data, we estimated the association between updated interval mean hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and mortality using Poisson regression to estimate mortality rates adjusted for age and sex and rate ratios adjusted for age, calendar year, sex, BMI, pulmonary function, and use of CF transmembrane conductance regulator modulators.

Of 4,477 individuals contributing 31,311 person-years of follow-up, 758 died. Mortality rates increased progressively with higher updated interval mean HbA1c values. Compared with HbA1c ≤42 mmol/mol, adjusted mortality rate ratios were 1.41 (95% CI 1.15-1.73) for HbA1c >42-53 mmol/mol, 1.66 (95% CI 1.33-2.07) for HbA1c >53-69 mmol/mol, and 1.93 (95% CI 1.53-2.43) for HbA1c >69 mmol/mol.
Higher HbA1c was associated with a clinically and statistically significant increase in mortality among individuals with CF-related diabetes.

Article.ArticleTitle: Metadherin Drives FOXO3a Lactylation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction to Promote Podocyte Injury in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study investigated whether metadherin (MTDH) drives podocyte injury in diabetic kidney disease through metabolic reprogramming. We sought to define the molecular mechanisms linking altered glucose metabolism to podocyte mitochondrial dysfunction. We found that MTDH upregulates lactate dehydrogenase A, leading to lactate-driven FOXO3a lactylation that selectively activates proapoptotic genes and disrupts pyruvate kinase M2-mitofusin 2 interaction, impairing mitochondrial fusion. These findings identify MTDH as a central metabolic regulator and suggest that targeting MTDH-mediated pathways, including FOXO3a lactylation and pyruvate kinase M2-mitofusin 2 disruption, may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for diabetic kidney disease.

Article.ArticleTitle: Safety of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors in Older Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Cohort Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in individuals with type 2 diabetes, but safety data in older adults remain limited. We evaluated the real-world safety of SGLT2is compared with dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors (DPP-4is) among individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes.

We conducted a population-based, active-comparator, new-user cohort study using administrative health databases from British Columbia, Canada. We included individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes initiating SGLT2is or DPP-4is between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2023. Primary outcomes were infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, fall, fracture, and all-cause hospitalization. Cox regression with propensity score-based standardized mortality ratio weighting was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs).

The study included 4,997 SGLT2i initiators (median age, 79 years; 37% women) and 1,289 DPP-4i initiators (median age, 82 years; 50% women). Compared with DPP-4i initiation, SGLT2i initiation was associated with lower risks of acute kidney injury (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60-0.95) and all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77-0.98), with no difference in risk of infection. No differences were observed in risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, falls, or fractures, although CIs were compatible with both benefit and harm.

In individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2i initiation was not associated with increased risk of harm compared with DPP-4i initiation, although estimates were imprecise for some outcomes. These findings may support consideration of SGLT2is as a treatment option in this population.

Article.ArticleTitle: Target Trial of Semaglutide Versus Dulaglutide or Liraglutide in Patients Receiving Hemodialysis.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients with diabetes receiving maintenance hemodialysis.

Using 2011-2022 U.S. Renal Data System and Medicare data, we emulated a target trial evaluating semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients receiving hemodialysis. Overlap weights were used to adjust for confounders. Fine-Gray models were used to assess death on dialysis and hospitalization. A generalized estimating equation was used for repeated measures of body weight.

We identified 1,312 semaglutide and 2,601 dulaglutide or liraglutide users. After overlap weighting, the effective sample size was 3,200 patients (mean age 61; 63% White; 28% Black; 52% male; median [interquartile range] BMI 34 [29-40] kg/m2; median follow-up 1.1 [0.6-1.9] years). Semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide was associated with a mortality on dialysis subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) of 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.97; 1-year cumulative incidence 11% vs. 13%) and all-cause hospitalization sHR of 0.91 (95% CI 0.83-0.99; 1-year incidence 57% vs. 62%). Body weight loss was higher with semaglutide (-4.8%, 95% CI -5.3% to -4.2%) at 1 year vs. -3.4%, 95% CI -3.9% to -3.1%). Direct comparisons of semaglutide versus dulaglutide showed similar results for mortality (sHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69-0.97) and hospitalization (sHR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.97), but semaglutide versus liraglutide showed no statistically significant benefit for mortality or hospitalization.

Among patients with diabetes receiving hemodialysis and equipoise between semaglutide and dulaglutide or liraglutide, semaglutide may be the preferred glucagon-like peptide 1 agent compared with dulaglutide.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Phase 2, Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Acmopatide (CT-868), a Fully Biased GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonist, in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes and Overweight or Obesity.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of acmopatide, a signal-biased glucagon-like peptide 1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonist, in adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and overweight/obesity.

In this phase 2, 16-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study, adults with T1D (HbA1c 7.0-10.0%; BMI ≥27 kg/m2) were randomized 1:1:1:1 to once-daily subcutaneous acmopatide (1.8, 4.1, or 6.6 mg) or volume-matched placebo. The primary end point was change from baseline (CFB) in HbA1c (%) at week 16; secondary end points included percent CFB in body weight and insulin dose.

Overall, 111 participants were randomized (placebo n = 29, acmopatide 1.8 mg n = 27, 4.1 mg n = 28, 6.6 mg n = 27). Mean (SD) baseline HbA1c was 7.5% (0.6), and mean BMI was 34.3 (5.6) kg/m2. Acmopatide improved HbA1c (least squares [LS] mean CFB -0.4 to -0.6% vs. -0.3% with placebo; nominally significant placebo-adjusted difference for 4.1 mg: -0.3% [90% CI -0.6 to -0.1]; P = 0.020). HbA1c <7.0% was achieved by 55.6% of participants receiving acmopatide 4.1 mg vs. 33.3% receiving placebo. Acmopatide-treated participants demonstrated reductions in body weight (LS mean CFB -3.3 to -6.7% vs. 0.3% with placebo; all P < 0.01), total daily insulin dose (-3.4 to -14.9% more than placebo for acmopatide 4.1 and 6.6 mg), and mean systolic blood pressure (-3.1 to -8.4 mmHg vs. -3.3 mmHg with placebo). Adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal. No diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or severe hypoglycemia events occurred.
In adults with T1D and overweight/obesity, acmopatide was associated with improved glycemic control and clinically meaningful weight loss without DKA or severe hypoglycemia events.

Article.ArticleTitle: Gene-by-Sleep Duration Interaction for Glycemic Traits in More Than 480,000 Individuals.

Abstract.AbstractText: The biological mechanisms of how sleep duration impacts type 2 diabetes pathogenesis and glycemic control are unclear. This study reveals 16 loci (11 novel) that interact with either short or long sleep duration to influence hemoglobin A1c, fasting glucose, or fasting insulin. Short and long sleep duration loci were nonoverlapping. Regulation of copper and diacylglycerol levels appear as distinct cellular mechanisms implicated by long and short sleep duration loci, respectively. Identified gene targets present insight for potential type 2 diabetes therapeutic design approaches related to JIP1-c-Jun N-terminal kinase interaction disruption, pericyte health, N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor activity, anti-inflammatory and leptin-enhancing dietary supplements, and serpins.

Article.ArticleTitle: Reactions to Race[ism]: The Relationship Between Differential Treatment Based on Race and Diagnosed Diabetes Status in U.S. Adults.

Abstract.AbstractText: To examine associations between diabetes status and self-reported discrimination based on race among U.S. adults with and without diabetes.

We analyzed 2022-2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 328,056 adults completing the Reactions to Race module and reporting diabetes status. Experiences of racial discrimination at work, in health care, or elsewhere, and related physical symptoms, were categorized as any versus none. Weighted prevalence and multivariable logistic regression were stratified by diabetes status.

Discrimination based on race was reported by 14.2% of adults with diabetes and 12.5% without diabetes. Patterns were similar across age, metropolitan status, and employment subgroups. In both groups, discrimination was associated with race and ethnicity, age, sex, employment, poor mental health, and current smoking.

Experiences of racial discrimination were common among U.S. adults and were reported more frequently by adults with diabetes. Because discrimination can contribute to chronic stress, reduced access to high-quality care, and barriers to diabetes self-management, consideration of racism-related exposures is important in efforts to understand and address diabetes disparities.

Article.ArticleTitle: CYP1B1: A Context-Dependent Regulator of Metabolism in Diabetic Kidney Disease.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study systematically dissects the regulatory role of CYP1B1 in the pathogenesis of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). CYP1B1 participates in the progression of DKD by mediating the metabolism of arachidonic acid, retinoic acid, and estradiol, as well as the process of ferroptosis. Its 4-OHE2 quinone metabolites and proferroptotic effect promote renal injury, while it is associated with the maintenance of renoprotective signaling. The net effect of CYP1B1 is regulated by substrate type, cell type, and disease stage, and it can serve as an epigenetic marker and gut-kidney axis mediator in DKD.

Article.ArticleTitle: Extracellular vesicles from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells protect grafted islets against endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction via modulating XBP1-based calcium homeostasis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Although islet transplantation is an ideal option for individuals with diabetes, early graft failure due to beta cell apoptosis and stress-induced dysfunction severely limits long-term efficacy. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hucMSCs) have multiple functions including maintaining cellular homeostasis. However, it remains unknown as to whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from hucMSCs (hucMSC-EVs) provide protective effects against transplant-related trauma-induced islet injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of hucMSC-EVs on islet graft survival in a syngeneic mouse model of islet transplantation and to examine the mechanism of protection.

EVs were isolated from cultured hucMSCs and characterised by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking and western blotting. The effects of hucMSC-EVs on islet graft function were evaluated in a mouse model of streptozocin-induced diabetes via co-transplantation under the kidney capsule. Beta cell survival and function were assessed by immunofluorescence, TUNEL staining, insulin secretion assays and in vivo imaging. Endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS) and mitochondrial dysfunction were further analysed in primary islets and NIT-1 beta cells under thapsigargin- or tunicamycin-stimulated ERS models. Further calcium imaging, JC-1 staining, western blotting and Seahorse assays were performed. microRNA sequencing was conducted and the role of miR-182-5p and XBP1 in mediating hucMSC-EV function was verified using knockdown, overexpression and dual-luciferase assays.

Co-transplantation of hucMSC-EVs with 250 islet equivalents significantly improved glycaemic control (p<0.01) and glucose tolerance (p<0.01) in diabetic mice. Apoptotic beta cells were significantly reduced in grafts receiving EVs, as shown by TUNEL assays (p<0.05) and cleaved caspase 3 staining (p<0.05). Ex vivo, hucMSC-EVs were internalised by beta cells and protected against tunicamycin-induced apoptosis (p<0.01), preserved insulin expression and restored glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. While ERS enhanced interactions between endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, hucMSC-EVs maintained calcium homeostasis, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism and alleviated ERS. Small RNA sequencing and functional analysis identified that XBP1-targeted miR-182-5p was enriched in hucMSC-EVs, which further fine-tuned endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria communication via reducing inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors at mitochondria-associated membranes and activated Nrf2 to restore mitochondrial calcium homeostasis under ERS. miR-182-5p inhibition reversed the protective effects of EVs on beta cell calcium homeostasis and viability. In vivo, depletion of miR-182-5p in hucMSC-EVs abolished the ability to prevent beta cell apoptosis and improve glycaemic control in diabetic mice.

hucMSC-EVs significantly improved the survival and function of islet grafts by delivering miR-182-5p, which targeted XBP1 to modulate mitochondria-associated membranes, attenuate ERS and restore mitochondrial calcium homeostasis. These findings highlight a novel cell-free EV-based therapeutic strategy for improving the outcome of islet transplantation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Clinical and metabolic subtypes of recent-onset adult type 1 diabetes: a prospective cohort study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Adult-onset type 1 diabetes exhibits substantial heterogeneity. We aimed to investigate whether this variability reflects distinct disease entities or different temporal stages of a shared autoimmune process.

In this prospective cohort study, we analysed data from adults (aged 18-69 years) in the German Diabetes Study who had clinically diagnosed type 1 diabetes within the preceding 12 months, and from individuals who were positive for glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (GADA) but had originally been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. We used unsupervised machine learning based on GADA status, fasting C-peptide, glucose, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol to characterise clinical and metabolic type 1 diabetes subtypes. The resulting subtypes were compared for aetiological traits (polygenic risk scores for type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes, partitioned type 2 diabetes polygenic risk scores, human leukocyte antigen [HLA] profiles, and islet-directed autoantibodies), insulin sensitivity, glucagon-stimulated C-peptide trajectories as a measure of residual β-cell function, and complications during prospective follow-up. Reproducibility was assessed in adults with type 1 diabetes from the German Diabetes Prospective Follow-up Registry (Diabetes-Patienten-Verlaufsdokumentation [DPV]).

Analysed participants in the German Diabetes Study cohort were recruited between June 27, 2005, and Jan 20, 2025 (n=600), and were followed up for a mean of 6·1 (SD 4·7) years. We identified three type 1 diabetes subtypes: two GADA-positive subtypes, and one GADA-negative subtype. A similar clinical and metabolic subtype structure was observed in the DPV cohort, whose participants were recruited between 2000 and 2025 (n=483) and were followed up for a mean of 3·1 (SD 5·0) years. One GADA-positive subtype was characterised by lower BMI, higher insulin sensitivity, and severe β-cell dysfunction (classic type 1 diabetes), whereas the second showed higher BMI, lower insulin sensitivity, and better β-cell function (mixed type 1 diabetes). The two GADA-positive subtypes did not differ in autoimmunity or type 1 diabetes polygenic risk scores, whereas the GADA-negative subtype had lower genetic type 1 diabetes risk, despite no clear subtype-specific differences in HLA risk haplotypes. Longitudinal modelling indicated that the mixed type 1 diabetes group was positioned 6·1 years (95% CI 4·6-7·8) earlier along the β-cell function decline trajectory compared with the classic type 1 diabetes group. The risks of hypoglycaemia (log-rank p=0·0019), retinopathy (mixed type 1 diabetes vs classic type 1 diabetes: adjusted hazard ratio 4·93 [95% CI 1·71-14·24]), and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (log-rank p=0·028) differed across the groups.

Our results indicate that individuals with combined autoimmunity and lower insulin sensitivity present with clinical diabetes earlier than classic type 1 diabetes along the β-cell decline trajectory, identifying a potential timeframe for disease-modifying interventions in specific type 1 diabetes subtypes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Orforglipron, a small-molecule, non-peptide, oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, has shown bodyweight reduction and cardiometabolic benefits in adults with obesity across phase 3 trials globally. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of orforglipron versus placebo for treating obesity disease in Japanese adults.

ATTAIN-J was a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 3 trial conducted across 16 medical research centres and hospitals in Japan and included adults aged 18 years or older with a BMI between 27 kg/m2 and less than 35 kg/m2 and two or more obesity-related health disorders, or a BMI of 35 kg/m2 or higher and one or more obesity-related health disorder, with one or more of the obesity-related health disorders being hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or type 2 diabetes (targeted at about 25% of participants), consistent with Japanese indications for tirzepatide and semaglutide for obesity disease; and at least one unsuccessful dietary attempt to lose weight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) via a computer-generated sequence to once-daily oral orforglipron (6 mg, 12 mg, or 36 mg) or placebo. Co-primary endpoints were mean percentage change in bodyweight and percentage of participants with at least 5% bodyweight reduction from baseline to week 72. Efficacy endpoints were primarily evaluated by the treatment regimen estimand in all randomly assigned participants. Safety was assessed in participants who received at least one dose of study treatment. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05931380 (completed).

Between July 31, 2023, and June 19, 2025, 291 participants were screened, of whom 238 (144 [61%] males and 94 [39%] females; mean age 54·1 years [SD 11·2]) were randomly assigned to receive orforglipron 6 mg (n=61), 12 mg (n=57), or 36 mg (n=60), or placebo (n=60); 214 (90%) participants completed the study. At week 72, mean percentage change in bodyweight was -5·9% (95% CI -7·6 to -4·2) with orforglipron 6 mg, -8·7% (-10·9 to -6·5) with 12 mg, and -7·9% (-10·0 to -5·8) with 36 mg, compared with -0·6% (-2·1 to 0·8) with placebo (all p<0·0001 vs placebo). At week 72, a bodyweight reduction of at least 5% was seen in 15·2% (SE 4·8; nine of 60) of participants in the placebo group compared with 45·6% (6·1; 28 of 61; p=0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 6 mg group, 60·8% (6·4; 35 of 57; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 12 mg group, and 58·8% (6·5; 35 of 60; p<0·0001) of participants in the orforglipron 36 mg group. Adverse events with orforglipron were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal symptoms. Across all orforglipron groups, treatment-emergent adverse events that most frequently led to study treatment discontinuation were nausea (one [2%] of 61 in the 6 mg group, one [2%] of 57 in the 12 mg group, and five [8%] of 60 in the 36 mg group vs none with placebo) and vomiting (none in the 6 mg group, two [4%] in the 12 mg group, and one [2%] in the 36 mg group vs none in the placebo group).

In Japanese adults with obesity disease, once-daily orforglipron resulted in statistically superior reductions in bodyweight versus placebo, with a safety profile consistent with that of other GLP-1 receptor agonists.
